topic: CUA-S1 review: a System One model purpose-built for computer use
keyword: cua s1 system one computer use
summary: CUA-S1 is trycua's (Cua AI, Inc.) family of small, specialist 'System One' models that score closed sets of (element, action) options in a single forward pass instead of generating action text token by token. It is not a computer-use agent: planning, option enumeration, ordering and execution all stay in the surrounding application code (optionally Cua Driver). Four checkpoints exist as of this review: cua-s1-forms / cua-s1-form-v0 (706,048 params, MIT), cua-s1-nano-0.1 (~855K params, from-scratch, Apache-2.0), cua-s1-4b-0.1 and cua-s1-4b-0.2 (LoRA rank 16 adapters on frozen Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B, Apache-2.0 adapters only). The honest headline is that Cua publishes unusually candid, calibrated evaluation data — and that data shows the 4B adapter winning decisively on the families it trained on while scoring at or below chance on chess and game control, and the tiny forms model answering a high-confidence 'skip' on 29.3% of out-of-catalogue held-out forms. The GitHub component is a source-only research release; weights live on Hugging Face.

key_facts.vendor: Cua AI, Inc. (trycua) — founded/led publicly by Francesco Bonacci (frabonacci) and Dillon
key_facts.repo: https://github.com/trycua/cua (MIT, 27,087 stars, 1,889 forks, 1,042 open issues as of 2026-09-29)
key_facts.release_model: Source-only research release; no weights, datasets, demo binaries or recordings in the repo. Weights hosted separately on Hugging Face.
key_facts.family_positioning: CUA-S1 sits beside Cua Driver (cross-OS desktop automation), Cua Fleets (isolated cloud desktops), Lume (local macOS/Linux VMs on Apple Silicon) and Cua Bench (task authoring + evaluation).
key_facts.system_one_analogy: Cua's own wording: 'System 1' is an engineering analogy for fast, bounded decisions (which value goes in a field, whether to leave an element alone). It is explicitly not a strict model-architecture classification and not a replacement for a general-purpose agent's planning and reasoning.
key_facts.decoding_contract: Closed-set selection, not generation. For the 4B checkpoints a chat-template prompt asks for a single letter identifying the chosen option; each option letter is a verified single tokenizer token; one forward pass is run; final-position logits at the option-letter positions are softmaxed into per-option probabilities.
key_facts.lineage_vs_jevlike: The forms model uses jevlike's option-attention head; the model card for cua-s1-forms states it shares the same input/output contract as TypeSafe's Jev. Cua is explicit that cua-s1-forms is an independent research checkpoint, not a reproduction of Jev, and is not RLCD-calibrated.

competitors.name: TypeSafe AI — Introducing System One Models & Jev (2026-09-15)
key_points: Defines the 'System One Model' category this whole field is named after: fast, structured decisions that software can consume directly, rather than string generation.
Jev gives up string generation; the pitch is 'structured outputs and can't hallucinate' — a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out.
Introduces RLCD (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions) as the training method, framed against RLHF/RLVR, claiming epistemically honest probabilities.
Claims similar System One intelligence to existing LLMs while being two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient.
Jev is a hosted, early-access API — the proprietary baseline every open clone (including CUA-S1) is measured against.
competitors.why_competes: The category-defining incumbent and the hosted baseline in Cua's own benchmark tables.

competitors.name: Latent.Space / AINews — 'Here are 6 Clones of Jev in 2 days' (2026-09-19)
key_points: Documents the open-source wave that CUA-S1 belongs to, and why it happened: Jev was not open source, which invited speculation and reimplementations.

Names the field: Laya (421M, ModernBERT-large encoder plus two transformer layers, PPO over sequence embeddings), DiffusionGemmaJev, Bespoke Nimble (LoRA on Qwen3.5-9B), SemIf/OpenJev (4B and 35B Qwen3.5 backbone with a tiny three-class NLI head), Jevlike (40K byte-embedding option-attention model), Kev-0.5B.
Adoption data point: Vercel reported Jev reached ~13% of teams in day one, 2x the GPT-5.6 family and 6x Fable 5.1 on AI Gateway.
States the data side everyone acknowledges is 100% synthetic.
competitors.why_competes: The definitive competitive framing: CUA-S1 is one of ~6+ open System One efforts chasing one hosted incumbent.

competitors.name: Awesome Jev — community catalog (944 verified projects, snapshot 2026-09-18–28)
key_points: Independent, community-maintained index of 944 open-source projects across 11 categories, with a dedicated 'Jev-like models' section (72 entries) and 'Browser & computer use' (75).
Confirms the ecosystem size around System One models in the space of ~10 days, and that computer-use is one of its fastest-growing verticals.
Useful as evidence that 'small specialist decision model' is now a crowded design space, not a novelty.
competitors.why_competes: Not a model — it is the best single source showing how crowded CUA-S1's niche became within days.

competitors.name: cua-ai/cua-s1-forms (HF model + dataset card) — the first release
key_points: 706,048-parameter byte-level transformer (2-layer encoder, width 128, 4 heads) plus an option-attention head; 2.8 MB checkpoint; MIT.
Context truncated to 224 bytes per element; options one per document entity plus fixed check/click/skip, each truncated to 96 bytes.

Reported results (author-reported, not reproduced in libs/cua-s1): 99.95% top-1 on the synthetic form-disjoint test (~15k decisions), 100% on a 196-decision real demo set (3 real form pages + 3 real PDFs), 37% on a shuffled-context control.

Head-to-head on the same task: 99.7% for this model vs 83.6% for hosted Jev (jev-latest, no fine-tuning); hosted Jev scored 96% on judgement decisions and 74% on recognizing an already-filled field as a no-op.

Limitations it declares on itself: cannot invent a value, English-centric label vocabulary, trained entirely on synthetic forms, evaluated on only 196 real decisions, not RLCD-calibrated, no weights-backed CI or Cua Driver E2E for this checkpoint.
Security note: older revisions shipped a pickle .pt checkpoint; it was removed, and cua_s1 refuses pickle checkpoints by design (trycua/cua#3977).
competitors.why_competes: This is CUA-S1's actual first product. A review must separate the 706K demo-grade forms model from the 4B adapters.

competitors.name: cua-ai/cua-s1-4b-0.2 — the current flagship
key_points: Two separately trained LoRA adapters (rank 16) on frozen Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B — one text (accessibility tree), one multimodal (screenshot). 187 MB download; Apache-2.0 covers the adapters only.

Base model is 9.34 GB of 16-bit weights (two safetensors shards), so inference needs >9.3 GB of memory before activations. Cua states an 8 GB host cannot run it; plan on 16 GB free. Peak memory has not been measured.
Trained with a supervised stage and an RL stage (RLOO, per Cua's launch thread) against live GUI environments.
Does not replace cua-s1-4b-0.1; both remain published.
competitors.why_competes: The checkpoint a review titled 'a System One model purpose-built for computer use' should actually be judged on.

competitors.name: libs/cua-bench-s1 Results section — Cua's own measured benchmark tables
key_points: Publishes both raw and chance-corrected tables for jev, djev, semif, cua-s1-nano-0.1, cua-s1-4b-0.1 and cua-s1-4b-0.2, with a measured per-row p_chance and ECE reported.
Text hard cross-dataset (frozen 615-task GUI-360 split): cua-s1-4b-0.2 0.833-1.000 on five families, but 0.429 on pagination; cua-s1-4b-0.1 ranges 0.167-0.571; nano is 0.000 across the board.
Multimodal hard cross-dataset (frozen 168-task split, ax_tree stripped): cua-s1-4b-0.2 overall 0.929 (ECE 0.069) vs djev 0.601, semif 0.244.

Live agentic rollouts (cua-bench-basic, held-out variants 2-4, N=18, 20-step cap, success = terminal env reward): cua-s1-4b-0.2 text 0.944 / multimodal 0.722, djev 0.889 / 0.667, cua-s1-4b-0.1 text 0.000 / multimodal 0.333.
Cua documents its own failures: cua-s1-4b-0.1's text adapter collapses to 'skip' on 340/360 steps — its SFT removed agentic capability the zero-shot base already had.
chess and game_control show no measurable signal for any model once chance-corrected; the pagination row is flagged by Cua as a family-taxonomy labeling artifact, not a capability result.
Caveat published with the tables: hardware and batch size are not standardized across runs (jev is a hosted API round-trip; djev/semif ran on GPU; nano is CPU-fast).
competitors.why_competes: This is the primary evidence base for any serious review, and it is better than what most vendors publish.

angles: 'System One' is an analogy, not an architecture — Cua says so itself, and that candor is what makes the label survivable. A review should refuse the Kahneman framing as a spec and keep it as a design intent.

The real product is the decision interface, not the model: a closed, pre-enumerated option set plus a softmax over option logits. That is simultaneously the selling point (no hallucinated strings, one forward pass) and the hard limit (the model cannot propose an action nobody enumerated, and cannot be evidence that the option set was safe or complete).

Read the family, not the launch post: the 706K forms model and the 4B adapters are different products with different evidence. The launch narrative ('our first release is CUA-S1-FORMS') is about the tiny MIT demo; the benchmark story is about the 4B LoRA pair.

Cua's benchmark honesty is the standout feature — they publish raw AND chance-corrected tables, a measured p_chance per row, ECE, per-run dataset hashes, and they flag one of their own rows (pagination) as a labeling artifact. Almost no vendor does this. It also means the numbers cannot be read naively: a lot of rows are at or below chance.

The 29.3% out-of-catalogue failure is the most instructive result in the whole release. The tiny forms model does not abstain — it emits a high-confidence 'skip' (36 of 41 predictions, mean confidence 0.974). An executor that treats 'skip' as 'nothing to do here' will silently no-op an entire out-of-scope form. This is a general lesson about confidence as a safety signal.

Regression inside your own family: cua-s1-4b-0.1's text adapter collapses to 'skip' on 340/360 live steps while its zero-shot base already scored 0.333. SFT removed agentic capability. A second adapter generation (0.2) was needed to recover it — and 0.1 was kept published.

Cost shape is inverted from the pitch: the 4B adapters need a >9.3 GB base model and a 16 GB memory floor, and single decisions measured 1.07-2.83 s on an M1 Ultra — versus 0.003 s mean per-task for the 855K nano model, which scores 0.000 on the same families. You get cheap or correct, not both, in this family.

Deployment cost of the category, not just the model: options must be enumerated by the caller, the executor must order actions, and Cua's own security guidance says a specialist checkpoint 'is not a security boundary' and its outputs 'must not be used as authorization'. Human confirmation for consequential actions is stated policy, not optional.

The competitive frame is a race, not a product review: one hosted incumbent (Jev), 6+ named open reimplementations in 2 days, and 944 catalogued projects within ~10 days. Choosing CUA-S1 in 2026 is choosing a fast-moving research line with a real vendor behind it.

Artifact-integrity details worth a reviewer noting: safetensors + JSON only, pickle checkpoints rejected by design after #3977, a SHA-256 tensor signature validated before load, and per-checkpoint licences that differ (MIT for forms, Apache-2.0 for nano and the 4B adapters, Qwen's own licence for the base).

key_data_points.positioning: NOT an agent. A closed-set option scorer that replaces the per-step 'which element, which action' LLM call; planning/ordering/execution stay in caller code.
four_checkpoints: cua-s1-form-v0 / cua-s1-forms — 706,048 params, tinyx byte-level transformer + option-attention, MIT, 2.8 MB
cua-s1-nano-0.1 — 855,296 params from scratch, text + multimodal (SmolVLM-256M or SigLIP) contexts, Apache-2.0, 6.9 MB
cua-s1-4b-0.1 — LoRA rank 16 on frozen Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B, text + multimodal adapters, Apache-2.0 adapters, 272 MB
cua-s1-4b-0.2 — separately trained pair of LoRA adapters on the same frozen base, SFT + RL (RLOO) stages against live GUI environments, 187 MB; does NOT replace 0.1
key_data_points.evidence_quality: Raw + chance-corrected tables, measured p_chance per row, ECE, dataset hashes, published per-run eval_results directories. But hardware/batch is not standardized across runs.
key_data_points.best_results: Multimodal hard cross-dataset overall 0.929 (ECE 0.069) for 0.2; general_decision zero-shot 0.887; live agentic episodes 0.944 text / 0.722 multimodal.
key_data_points.worst_results: chess and game_control at or below chance after correction for every model; OSWorld next-action task accuracy <=0.083 for all; 0.1's text adapter 0.000 on live episodes (skip collapse, 340/360 steps).
key_data_points.safety_position_vendor: SECURITY.md: treat screen content, documents and model-generated actions as untrusted; isolate runtime; least privilege; require human confirmation for consequential/irreversible/privileged/external actions; the checkpoint 'is not a security boundary' and its output is not authorization.
key_data_points.honest_caveat_from_vendor: README: none of the checkpoints 'should be treated as a general-purpose assistant or as evidence of reliable performance outside its evaluated task and environment boundaries.'

notes_for_writer: This is a REVIEW: take a position. The defensible verdict is positive-with-boundaries — Cua publishes the most honest evaluation data in the System One field, the 4B adapters are genuinely strong on the six GUI families they target, and everything outside that envelope is either at chance or actively dangerous to trust (the high-confidence skip).
Do not describe CUA-S1 as a computer-use agent. It is a per-step decision scorer. The agent is your code plus Cua Driver.
Be careful with the forms numbers: 99.95% synthetic / 100% on 196 real decisions are AUTHOR-REPORTED and explicitly not reproduced by libs/cua-s1. Always attach that caveat.

The single most quotable technical detail is the 29.3% held-out accuracy with 36 of 41 predictions being 'skip' at mean confidence 0.974 — and that re-labeling with in-catalogue wording restored accuracy to 11/11. That is a clean demonstration that these models key on label vocabulary, not semantics.
Use at most two 'System 1 vs System 2' references and immediately restate Cua's own disclaimer that it is an engineering analogy, not an architecture claim.
Latency numbers come from one Apple M1 Ultra host (128 GB) and a GitHub ubuntu-latest runner; say so. Do not generalize to 'fast on any laptop' — an 8 GB machine cannot run the 4B at all.
